narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 73.8% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your class rank at the end of your third year was the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Being in the bottom decile (1 out of 10) compared to an average of about 5.8 among accepted students signaled that your academic performance was significantly below the level the model associates with passing the bar. Your LSAT score of 26 was the second most important factor and also pulled the prediction toward failure; it sits well below the average of 37 among students who were admitted. Your undergraduate GPA of 2.90 was the third most influential feature, but it worked in the opposite direction, slightly lowering the predicted risk of failure. However, this positive effect was not large enough to offset the other two.

In short, the combination of a very low class ranking and a low LSAT score outweighed your solid undergraduate GPA in the model’s eyes.

What you should do next is focus on improving the areas the model weighed most heavily. Retaking the LSAT and aiming for a substantially higher score, while also strengthening your academic performance in any remaining coursework, would be the most direct ways to change future predictions in your favor. Consider reaching out to the admissions office to discuss how they weigh these factors and whether additional evidence of your potential could be considered.
